desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a pregnant woman referred after a high-chance NIPT result for a rare autosomal trisomy, then interpreting her NIPT, ultrasound and booking blood reports, explaining why the result is not diagnostic, advising on confirmatory testing, answering her question about a relative's failed NIPT and safety-netting.
diagnosis: Differential: true fetal rare autosomal trisomy vs confined placental mosaicism / false-positive NIPT result
explain:
What NIPT is

Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) analyses cell-free DNA in maternal blood. Most of this DNA comes from the placenta (trophoblast), with a smaller part from the mother. It is a screening test: it estimates the chance of common chromosomal conditions (trisomy 21, 18, 13 and sex chromosome conditions) and, depending on the test, may also report rare autosomal aneuploidies (RAAs) or copy number variants. It does not diagnose.

Interpreting Hannah's reports

The NIPT is low chance for the common trisomies and sex chromosome conditions, and high chance for trisomy 16, an RAA. The fetal fraction of 9% is adequate, so this is a valid screening result, not a test failure. The 12-week scan is normal (nuchal translucency 1.6 mm, no structural abnormality seen), which is encouraging but does not exclude a chromosomal problem. She is RhD positive, so anti-D is not needed after an invasive procedure, and her blood-borne virus screen is negative.

Why a high-chance result may not mean an affected fetus

Because the DNA is largely placental, the test can detect a chromosomal change that is confined to the placenta (confined placental mosaicism, CPM) when the fetus is chromosomally normal. Other causes include a vanishing twin and maternal chromosomal changes. High-chance results must always be confirmed by diagnostic testing (CVS or amniocentesis) before any irreversible decision.

Rare autosomal aneuploidies (RAAs)

In NIPT reporting, RAAs are trisomies of chromosomes other than 13, 18 and 21 (for example trisomy 16). Full (non-mosaic) trisomy 16 in the fetus is not compatible with survival and is a common cause of first-trimester miscarriage, so an ongoing pregnancy with a normal 12-week scan makes it unlikely. The realistic explanations are CPM, which is the most common, or mosaic trisomy 16 in the fetus, which can be associated with growth restriction and structural anomalies such as heart defects. CPM involving chromosome 16 is linked with placental dysfunction (fetal growth restriction, pre-eclampsia and preterm birth), so growth surveillance with serial scans is needed even if the fetus is chromosomally normal. A trisomy rescue event may cause uniparental disomy (UPD), which matters mainly for the chromosomes that carry imprinted genes (6, 7, 11, 14, 15 and 20); for chromosome 16 the main concern is placental function and any trisomic cells in the fetus, and the genetic counsellor advises on further testing.

CVS or amniocentesis?

For an RAA, amniocentesis is preferred because the placenta is likely to be affected, which would confound a CVS result (CPM versus a true fetal abnormality). Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid containing fetal cells and is usually performed from about 15 weeks. For trisomy 13 and 18, CPM is also relatively common, so amniocentesis is generally preferred; if CVS is chosen, a mosaic or positive result may need amniocentesis to clarify. The procedure-related miscarriage risk is small (under 1%) and should be explained in plain terms.

Failed NIPT (no result)

A NIPT "no result" (test failure) is not reassuring. The chance of aneuploidy is higher in these pregnancies, particularly with a low fetal fraction. The woman should be offered counselling, a detailed ultrasound and diagnostic testing. A repeat NIPT is an option but must not delay diagnostic testing.

Counselling, follow-up and safety netting

Counselling should be non-directive, in plain language, without assuming what the woman will decide. Check what she understands, acknowledge emotion, avoid false reassurance and false alarm, give her time, involve genetic counselling and fetal medicine, and arrange early review and psychological support. If she is RhD negative, anti-D should be given after an invasive procedure. She should seek urgent care for bleeding, pain, fluid loss or fever, now or after a procedure.
focus: Counselling after a high-risk NIPT result
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. In Part 2 the candidate may explain the reports to Hannah directly; Hannah follows her Part 2 cues, and the examiner asks any question the candidate has not already covered. Hannah must ask about her sister's result before the end. A high-performing candidate checks what Hannah understands before explaining, takes a focused history (pregnancy so far, bleeding or pain, obstetric and family history, RhD status, her fears) and checks her wellbeing and the fetal heart. In Part 2 they correct the belief that NIPT is diagnostic, explain that the DNA tested is mostly placental so confined placental mosaicism can cause a high-chance result in an unaffected baby, define a rare autosomal trisomy, explain why amniocentesis is preferred to CVS here, arrange genetic counselling, fetal medicine review and a detailed ultrasound, answer the sister's "no result" question directly without false reassurance, and stay non-directive throughout.

A borderline candidate explains that the result needs confirmation and offers a diagnostic test, but does not explain why the result can be a false positive or why amniocentesis is preferred, or reassures her about the sister's "no result". They may give directive advice about the pregnancy, use jargon, or give an incomplete explanation of the risks and the process.
patient:
Role: You are Hannah Doyle, a 36-year-old accountant, 12 weeks and 4 days pregnant, in the hospital early pregnancy and fetal medicine clinic. You are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. You are anxious and tearful but cooperative. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "My GP rang yesterday and said my blood test showed a high chance of something called trisomy 16. I read online that it means my baby has a fatal condition."

History (give only when asked):

  • This pregnancy is planned and very wanted, conceived naturally. Your dates from your last period matched the 12-week scan, and the sonographer said the scan looked normal.
  • Your GP arranged the NIPT at 11 weeks because you are over 35 and wanted reassurance.
  • No vaginal bleeding, no abdominal pain and no fluid loss. Mild nausea in the mornings; eating and drinking normally.
  • Previous pregnancy: a healthy daughter, now 3, born vaginally at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. No miscarriages.
  • Medical history: nil. Medicines: a pregnancy multivitamin with folic acid and iodine. Allergies: none.
  • Blood group: "The booking bloods said A positive."
  • Family history: no known chromosomal or genetic conditions on either side. Your sister had the same test last year (see the question below). If asked, her baby was born healthy and she hopes to have another.
  • Social: you live with your partner, Sam, who is supportive and knows about the result. You have not told anyone else. Non-smoker; no alcohol since you found out you were pregnant.

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • You assumed the NIPT tests the baby's DNA and gives a definite answer. You read online that "trisomy 16 is always fatal".
  • Your friend had a CVS in her last pregnancy and miscarried a few weeks afterwards, so you are afraid of any procedure.
  • You have no strong views yet about the outcome of the pregnancy. You want time and information, and you want to be told what the doctor thinks is best.
points: NIPT is a screening test on cell-free DNA in maternal blood, most of which comes from the placenta; a high-chance result is not a diagnosis and needs confirmation by CVS or amniocentesis before any decision.
A high-chance result can occur in an unaffected fetus because of confined placental mosaicism (and other causes, such as a vanishing twin).
Rare autosomal aneuploidies (RAAs) are trisomies other than 13, 18 and 21; amniocentesis is preferred for confirmation because the placenta is likely to be affected and would confound a CVS result.
A failed NIPT (no result) is not reassuring: offer counselling, detailed ultrasound and diagnostic testing; a repeat NIPT is an option but must not delay diagnosis.
Counsel non-directively, avoid false reassurance, and arrange genetic counselling, fetal medicine review and follow-up.

stem: You are a junior doctor in a hospital early pregnancy and fetal medicine outpatient clinic. Hannah Doyle, a 36-year-old woman who is 12 weeks and 4 days pregnant, has been referred urgently by her GP after the result of her non-invasive prenatal test (NIPT).
tasks: Take a focused history from Hannah, including what she understands about the test, and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the NIPT report, her 12-week ultrasound report and her booking blood results. Interpret them and explain them to Hannah, then outline your management approach, including the options for diagnostic testing, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: High-chance NIPT result for a rare autosomal trisomy

part2.lead: Here is Hannah's NIPT report, the report of her 12-week ultrasound and her booking blood results. You may explain them to Hannah directly.

handover.result:

handover.model:
1. Read: a valid result (fetal fraction 9%, adequate), low chance for trisomies 21, 18 and 13 and the sex chromosome conditions, and a high chance of trisomy 16, a rare autosomal trisomy (a trisomy of a chromosome other than 13, 18 or 21).
  2. Meaning: NIPT screens cell-free DNA in Hannah's blood, most of which comes from the placenta, so it gives a chance, not a diagnosis. Full trisomy 16 in a baby almost always ends in early miscarriage, so with an ongoing pregnancy and a normal scan the likeliest explanation is confined placental mosaicism (the placenta carries the trisomy, the baby does not). Mosaic trisomy 16 in the baby, a vanished twin and a maternal chromosomal change are the other explanations.
  3. What it changes: no decision about the pregnancy rests on this result. Genetic counselling and fetal medicine review; amniocentesis offered from about 15 weeks (CVS samples the placenta, which is likely to carry the trisomy, so it could mislead); a detailed anatomy scan; and growth scans later in pregnancy, because placental trisomy 16 can affect how the placenta works even if the baby's chromosomes are normal.

handover.label: Ultrasound at 12 weeks 1 day
handover.result:
Examination: first trimester ultrasound, transabdominal, at 12 weeks 1 day by last menstrual period.

Clinical details: dating and nuchal translucency. Maternal age 36, G2 P1.

Findings:

  • Uterus: a single intrauterine gestational sac. No second sac seen.
  • Fetus: single live fetus, heart rate 158 bpm and regular. Crown-rump length 58 mm, in keeping with 12 weeks 1 day; dates confirmed.
  • Nuchal translucency 1.6 mm (within the normal range for this crown-rump length). Nasal bone present.
  • Anatomy at this gestation: skull ossified with a normal outline; midline falx and choroid plexuses seen; heart on the left with four chambers seen; stomach and bladder in normal position; anterior abdominal wall intact at the cord insertion; spine appears intact; four limbs seen moving.
  • Placenta posterior. Amniotic fluid normal. Both ovaries normal; no free fluid.

Conclusion: single live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with dates. Nuchal translucency 1.6 mm, within normal limits. No structural abnormality seen at this gestation; a detailed anatomy scan at 18 to 20 weeks is recommended.
handover.model:
Read: one live baby in one sac, dated correctly (crown-rump length 58 mm, 12 weeks 1 day), nuchal translucency 1.6 mm (normal), nasal bone present and no structural abnormality seen at 12 weeks.

Meaning: encouraging, and it fits a placental rather than a fetal cause for the NIPT result, but a normal 12-week scan does not exclude mosaic trisomy 16 or later problems such as growth restriction or a heart defect. No second sac makes a vanished twin less likely, although an early loss can leave no trace.

What it changes: it does not replace diagnostic testing. Hannah still needs genetic counselling, the offer of amniocentesis, a detailed anatomy scan with fetal medicine and growth scans in the third trimester.

handover.label: Booking blood tests
handover.model:
Read: haemoglobin 128 g/L, normal for the first trimester, with normal indices and platelets; blood group A RhD positive with no red cell antibodies; rubella immune; syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV not detected.

Meaning: nothing here bears on the NIPT result. RhD positive means anti-D is not needed after amniocentesis or CVS, and the negative blood-borne virus results mean no added risk of passing an infection to the baby during a needle procedure.

What it changes: amniocentesis can be offered without anti-D or extra precautions; routine antenatal care continues.

ask: What do these reports show, and what can NIPT not tell Hannah?
Why might the result be high chance when the baby does not have trisomy 16, and how would you explain this to her?
What is your management approach? Hannah asks why she cannot just have a CVS now, since it is earlier.
Hannah asks: "My sister had the same test last year and it came back as no result. Her doctor said not to worry. Is that right?" What do you tell her?
What follow-up and safety netting would you arrange?
part2.patient:
In Part 2, if the candidate explains the result to you:

  • If they explain that it is a screening test, you are relieved but still scared. If they do not explain the limits of the test, ask: "So does my baby definitely have this?"
  • Ask: "Could the test be wrong? How could that happen?"
  • Ask: "Why can't I just have a CVS now, since it is earlier? My friend had one." If they recommend amniocentesis, ask about the risk of miscarriage and the timing.
  • You must ask this before the end of the station: "My sister had the same test last year and it came back as 'no result'. Her doctor said not to worry and that it probably meant everything was fine. Is that right?"
  • Ask: "What happens if the follow-up test shows a problem?"
  • If the candidate gives a directive opinion about continuing or ending the pregnancy, say: "I'm not sure I can decide that today."
